items.title: 4.8 Interconversion of potential energy and kinetic energy

source_refs.note: Topic 4.8 with Figs. 4.12 and 4.13 and Examples 4.5 and 4.6 (PDF 87-89, printed 84-86). The exercise (PDF 89-92) is not reproduced.

blocks.text: Consider a body of mass m at rest at a height h above the surface of the Earth (Fig. 4.12). At position A the body has PE = mgh and KE = 0. We release the body, and as it falls we can examine how the kinetic and potential energies associated with it interchange. At position B, when the body has fallen a distance x (ignoring air friction), PE = mg (h - x) and KE = (1/2) m vB^2. The velocity vB at B follows from vf^2 = vi^2 + 2gS with vf = vB, vi = 0 and S = x: vB^2 = 0 + 2gx = 2gx, therefore KE = (1/2) m (2gx) = mgx. The total energy at position B is PE + KE: total energy = mg (h - x) + mgx = mgh ... (4.19). At position C, just before the body strikes the Earth, PE = 0 and KE = (1/2) m vC^2, where vC^2 = vi^2 + 2gh = 2gh as vi = 0; so KE = (1/2) m vC^2 = (1/2) m x 2gh = mgh. Thus at point C the kinetic energy equals the original value of the potential energy of the body.

Actually, when a body falls its velocity increases, because it is accelerated by gravity; the increase in velocity increases its kinetic energy. On the other hand, as the body falls its height decreases and hence its potential energy decreases. Thus we see (Fig. 4.13) that loss in PE = gain in KE: mg (h1 - h2) = (1/2) m (v2^2 - v1^2) ... (4.20), where v1 and v2 are the velocities of the body at heights h1 and h2. This result is true only when the frictional force is not considered. If a frictional force f is present during the downward motion, a part of the PE is used in doing work against friction, equal to f h, and the remaining PE = mgh - f h is converted into KE: mgh - f h = (1/2) m v^2, or mgh = (1/2) m v^2 + f h ... (4.21). Thus loss in PE = gain in KE + work done against friction, and conversely loss of KE = gain in PE + work done against friction.

blocks.caption: Interconversion of potential energy and kinetic energy (original diagram after Figures 4.12 and 4.13 and topic 4.8).
blocks.long_description: A body released from a height starts with potential energy mgh and no kinetic energy; after falling a distance its speed squared is twice g times that distance, so its kinetic energy equals the potential energy it has lost and the total stays mgh, and just before landing all the energy is kinetic. In general the loss in potential energy between two heights equals the gain in kinetic energy when friction is absent; with friction a part of the lost potential energy, the friction force times the height, goes into work against friction and only the rest becomes kinetic energy, and the same bookkeeping holds in reverse for a body losing kinetic energy as it climbs. A coasting car therefore reaches the top of a rise slower, by the energy spent on the climb and on friction, and then runs on the level until friction has used up what remains, while an object landing slower than free fall reveals the average air friction that acted on it.

blocks.title: Example 4.5
blocks.text: A car weighing 1100 kg moves at 12 m s^-1. When it is at point P its engine stops. If the frictional force is 120 N, what is its velocity at point Q (1.5 m higher, 24 m along the road), and how far beyond Q will it go before coming to rest? Solution: the kinetic energy at P is partly converted into PE and partly used up in doing work against friction up to Q, so loss of KE = gain in PE + work against friction: (1/2) m (vi^2 - vf^2) = w h + f d, (1/2) x 1100 kg x (144 m^2 s^-2 - vf^2) = (1100 kg x 9.8 m s^-2 x 1.5 m) + 120 N x 24 m, 550 kg (144 m^2 s^-2 - vf^2) = 16170 kg m^2 s^-2 + 2880 kg m^2 s^-2, (144 m^2 s^-2 - vf^2) = 19050 / 550 = 34.6 m^2 s^-2, vf^2 = 144 - 34.6 = 109.4 m^2 s^-2. Velocity at Q: vf = sqrt(109.4) = 10.5 m s^-1. If the car stops at point R, then (1/2) m v^2 = f S: (1/2) x 1100 kg x 109.4 m^2 s^-2 = 120 kg m s^-2 x S, so S = 501 m approximately.

blocks.title: Example 4.6
blocks.text: An object of mass 3 kg falls from a height of 15 m and strikes the ground at 16 m s^-1. Calculate the average frictional force of the air. Solution: loss of PE = gain in KE + work done against friction; as vi = 0, w h = (1/2) m v^2 + f h: 3 kg x 9.8 m s^-2 x 15 m = (1/2) x 3 kg x (16 m s^-1)^2 + f x 15 m, 441 kg m^2 s^-2 = 384 kg m^2 s^-2 + 15 m x f, or f = (441 - 384) kg m^2 s^-2 / 15 m = 3.8 kg m s^-2 = 3.8 N.

blocks.prompt: A 200 g apple is lifted to 10 m and dropped; if 75% of the lifting work becomes KE by the time it lands, find its landing speed (numerical 4.10). A child on a swing rises from 0.5 m to 1.5 m; what is the maximum speed (MCQ 4.4)? Does a body falling through air keep its total mechanical energy (short question 4.3)?
blocks.explanation: Lifting work = mgh = 0.2 x 9.8 x 10 = 19.6 J; KE at landing = 0.75 x 19.6 = 14.7 J = (1/2)(0.2) v^2, so v = sqrt(147) = 12.1 m s^-1. Loss in PE = gain in KE: v = sqrt(2 g x 1.0) = sqrt(19.6) = 4.4 m s^-1. No: part of the PE is spent as work against air friction, so the mechanical energy (PE + KE) falls by f h; only the total including heat is conserved.

items: Falling from h: at A PE = mgh, KE = 0; at B (fallen x) PE = mg(h - x), KE = mgx, total mgh (4.19); at C KE = mgh. Loss in PE = gain in KE: mg(h1 - h2) = (1/2) m (v2^2 - v1^2) (4.20), no friction.
With friction: mgh = (1/2) m v^2 + f h (4.21); loss in PE = gain in KE + work against friction, and the reverse for a climbing body. Examples: 10.5 m s^-1 at Q and 501 m to rest; air friction 3.8 N.
